articles.title: Mapping the siege of Yemen’s Taiz, and the price families are paying
articles.summary: Three weeks into the siege of Yemen’s third-largest city, prices have doubled, and families are down to the basics.
articles.body:
Taiz, Yemen – In the besieged city of Taiz, Yousef Farhan’s family has run out of choices at mealtime.

“The whole day, we either eat rice or beans, whether in the morning or in the evening,” the 39-year-old father of four told Al Jazeera.

Shelling forced the family from their home years ago, and they have lived in a school in Taiz’s Wadi al-Qadi zone ever since.

Farhan used to sell cucumbers from a small cart in front of the school, earning between 4,000 and 5,000 Yemeni riyals (roughly $2.50 to $3.20) a day. The money was never steady, but it bought a gas cylinder each month and, now and then, a meal with some variety.

Then the siege closed the school, and his trade went with it. The family now cooks over firewood.

“With the suspension of the school due to the shelling and the siege, my source of income stopped, and I was unable to find alternative work since the siege caused many people’s jobs to come to a halt,” he said.

His children, aged five months to five years, depend on whatever he can find. So do his sister and her child, who joined him after their neighbourhood came under fire.

Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, is home to about 1 million of the country’s roughly 43 million people.

The city has been cut off since early October, when it lost both of its land routes. The Houthis took the town of al-Turbah by October 4, severing the Taiz-Al-Turbah-Aden Road, the main artery for goods.

A day earlier, forces loyal to the internationally recognised government closed the eastern al-Houban crossing into Houthi-held territory, citing attempted Houthi incursions.

On October 20, the United Nations warned that road closures and lack of security were blocking vital supplies.

Prices of the food and fuel still available had more than doubled, and Taiz’s water production had dropped by half.

Across Taiz, families like Farhan’s are working out what to eat and whether they can afford to cook it.

The map below shows the main Taiz-Al-Turbah-Aden Road and three other routes out of the city, all now closed.

For weeks, 40-year-old Sayyun Burhan has looked no further ahead than tomorrow.

“We barely live day-to-day, waiting to see how the next day will pass,” she said.

Work is no longer available at the local store where Sayyun’s husband was employed, and his failing health makes it harder for him to find anything else. Meanwhile, the family still needs money for rent, food, water and cooking gas.

Across the city, the cost of water delivered by tankers has roughly tripled since the fighting escalated, according to UN officials.

The strain reaches beyond the kitchen. For Burhan’s children, the siege means missed lessons and long days inside, as she is afraid to let them out.

“They have been deprived of schooling and play,” she said.

Keeping both children safe and fed is becoming harder.

Fuel is behind many of Taiz’s civilian emergencies. Diesel keeps water pumps working, hospital generators running and ambulances moving. Petrol enables people can get to work, and patients to treatment. Cooking gas lets families and restaurants prepare food.

But the city’s fuel stations have been closed since October 5.

Prices gathered by Al Jazeera in Taiz show how sharply fuel costs have risen. A 20-litre (5.3-gallon) container of petrol now costs 120,000 riyals ($77), four times last year’s price of 30,000 riyals ($19).

The price of 20 litres of diesel has nearly doubled, from 46,000 riyals ($29) to 90,000 riyals ($58). A cooking gas cylinder has risen from 11,400 riyals ($7) to 40,000 riyals ($26).

Bus fares have risen from 200 riyals (13 cents) to 500 riyals (32 cents), an increase of 150 percent. Every ride now takes a bigger share of household budgets already stretched by rising food prices.

For Farhan, the move to firewood shows how far his family’s spending power has fallen. He once managed with a gas cylinder each month. Now, even a pot of rice or beans depends on what he can burn.

Water shortages are not new in Taiz, but the siege has made them worse. Diesel shortages have disrupted the pumps.

Local authorities say access restrictions are also stopping tankers from the Al-Dhabab basin, an important source of drinking water, from entering the city.

Fatima Khaled, 55, has kidney failure. She cannot afford repeated trips from her village west of the city to the hospital for treatment, or a room closer to the hospital. She sleeps on the floor of the dialysis hall at Al-Jumhuri General Hospital.

Closed roads and long mountain detours have made every journey for treatment exhausting and expensive.

The hospital itself is under strain. On October 22, the World Health Organization warned that 42 health facilities in Taiz were reporting severe shortages of fuel, oxygen, medicine and medical supplies.

“I feel like I am imprisoned here. We have no housing or shelter here. This hall is our shelter,” Fatima says.

articles.title: ​An old Brisbane hospital outbuilding was transformed into a five-bedroom home, with its industrial sawtooth roof and exposed brick left intact; the unique home on a 1,008 sq m plot sells for A$4.45 million
articles.summary: Ask people in the neighbourhood what 24 Brisbane Street used to be, and most will remember it as something else.
articles.body: Ask people in the neighbourhood what 24 Brisbane Street used to be, and most will remember it as something else. The property is now a five-bedroom home, but for years it was a hospital outbuilding, a working space with a purpose that had little to do with family dinners or weekend pool parties. Over time, it was reshaped, rebuilt and rethought until it became a place people actually live. The five-bedroom home in Annerley has finally found a buyer. Set on an elevated 1,008 sq m allotment, the home has sold for A$4.45 million, setting a suburb record, The Courier-Mail reported.A home with an industrial heritageThe first thing you notice at 24 Brisbane Street is the roof. Its sawtooth peaks throw light across hardwood floors recycled from older buildings. Nothing about the space looks as though it was built in one go. It looks like a building that has lived several lives. And it indeed has. It used to be a hospital outbuilding before architect Ric DeLuca turned it into ‘an extraordinary inner-city residence’, according to the listing on Domain.com.au. The architect did not gut-renovate it. Instead, he retained the sawtooth roofline, exposed brick and original structure, which gave the building a unique identity. None of these features could be replicated, so they had to stay.A home with ‘warehouse volume’The home sits on a 1,008 sq m plot, which is large for an inner-south property. Rather than building upwards, the house spreads across the site, creating a sense of openness. The listing describes its ‘warehouse volume’ and ‘unparalleled sense of space’ as defining features. While the home is spacious, it also provides the privacy every buyer seeks."Warehouse conversions are sought after because they have a sense of volume and personality that new homes cannot replicate, but few offer this amount of flexible living. It’s a home for buyers who want something completely different, but still need space for a family, visitors, multigenerational living or an additional income stream,​"​ Place New Farm lead agent and partner Heath Williams, who listed the home last month, told Realestate.com at the time.The house has several living and dining areas spread throughout, with a wood-burning fireplace set against the brick and wide timber doors that open onto terraces. Those terraces lead down to a 9 m pool surrounded by trees that have had years to grow. The layout works for more than one household. The main residence has three bedrooms and a master suite with a walk-through dressing room and a study. A separate wing has two more bedrooms, a kitchen, a living area and its own bathroom. That wing can operate independently, making it suitable for families with relatives to host or guests who want their own space.The kitchen is where the building’s past shines. It has Calacatta marble, two-pac cabinetry, Miele appliances and a Zanussi commercial oven. A walk-in butler’s pantry sits nearby, along with a large cold room. A serious cook would not need much convincing!The lower level holds a billiards room, a wine cellar and a laundry. Parking accommodates seven cars, three of them in a lock-up garage. Inside, a Control4 system runs the audiovisual setup, while a 19 kW solar system helps with the power bills.​A record saleThe home did not take long to find a buyer. It sold for A$4.45 million, a record for the suburb, according to multiple reports. The listing attracted multiple offers. ​"Each has its own X-factor,​" Williams told the paper. The price reflects something buyers cannot easily find elsewhere. He pushed back against the frequent use of the word ‘unique’ in property descriptions. The homes that matter, in his view, have character, history or design that cannot be copied or replicated. He also commented on buyer behaviour: ​"Buyers still have FOMO, but it’s more specific now.​"Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: Weight-loss drug could help address nighttime sleep disruptions for millions
articles.summary: Eli Lilly's retatrutide cut breathing interruptions and drove significant weight loss in sleep apnea patients, as well as cardiovascular benefits.
articles.body: An experimental obesity drug significantly reduced breathing interruptions and other symptoms of obstructive sleep disorder in two clinical trials, according to new research published in The New England Journal of Medicine. Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) affects more than 50 million Americans, and about 80% of cases are undiagnosed, according to the National Sleep Foundation. The study examined whether retatrutide, an investigational weight-loss drug from Eli Lilly, could help treat OSA in adults who were overweight or obese. EXPERIMENTAL OBESITY DRUG OUTPERFORMS TRADITIONAL WEIGHT-LOSS TREATMENTS IN EARLY RESEARCH Retatrutide is being evaluated in phase 3 TRIUMPH trials as a potential treatment for obesity and related metabolic conditions. The drug has not been approved by the FDA. The FDA has warned that unauthorized versions of retatrutide have been illegally marketed and sold online for weight loss. Study details The two phase 3 randomized trials included 691 adults with moderate-to-severe sleep apnea and a BMI of at least 27. Participants received once-weekly injections of retatrutide at doses of 4, 9 or 12 milligrams, or a placebo, and were followed for 80 weeks. The trials included 243 participants without type 2 diabetes and 448 with the condition. WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY FIGHT 7 SERIOUS HEALTH PROBLEMS BEFORE THE POUNDS EVEN COME OFF Participants who received retatrutide lost between 12% and nearly 20% of their body weight and experienced significantly fewer breathing interruptions than those who received a placebo. About 68% of participants experienced more than a 50% improvement in OSA symptoms, regardless of whether they had type 2 diabetes. The study also found that hypoxic burden — the severity and duration of low-oxygen episodes caused by breathing disruptions during sleep — fell by about 75% among participants without type 2 diabetes and 65% among those with the condition. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES The researchers concluded that retatrutide led to significantly greater reductions in AHI (breathing interruptions) than a placebo among adults with OSA who were obese or overweight, regardless of whether they had type 2 diabetes. The researchers noted that retatrutide’s lack of FDA approval was a limitation, and further studies are needed to determine how the drug may affect long-term cardiovascular outcomes. Expert reaction Study co-author Dr. Virend Somers, a cardiologist and professor of medicine at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, told Fox News Digital that while the results were expected, he was surprised by the "magnitude of benefit in patients with type 2 diabetes," as well as the significant reduction in sleep apnea. "OSA is often under-diagnosed and under-treated." "This is a very exciting time in treating sleep apnea patients," Somers said. Sleep apnea is associated with a higher risk of heart attacks, strokes, high blood pressure and atrial fibrillation. In the trial, participants experienced reductions in several cardiovascular risk factors, including systolic blood pressure, LDL cholesterol, systemic inflammation and neck circumference. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "A reduction in these measures would predict whether these patients were at increased cardiovascular risk," Somers told Fox News Digital. "In diabetics, blood pressure is a key determinant of future cardiovascular risk, and the fact that we were able to reduce it so significantly was both surprising and exciting." Somers said retatrutide also improved several diabetes-related measures. In participants without diabetes, insulin levels fell by more than 50%. Among those with type 2 diabetes, 40% progressed from diabetes to prediabetes and another 40% no longer met the criteria for diabetes, according to the researcher. The improvements were largely linked to weight loss, which can lead to better sleep and reduced sleep-related impairment, he said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "[The participants] reported much improved sleep beyond just the sleep apnea — what we call sleep-related impairment was significantly reduced," Somers said. The study included participants who were using CPAP and those who were not. Somers said CPAP use generally declined during the study, suggesting that some patients may eventually require less device-based treatment. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Dr. Wendy Troxel, a RAND senior behavioral scientist in Utah who was not involved in the study, noted that OSA is often under-diagnosed and under-treated, especially among postmenopausal women. "Although CPAP remains the frontline treatment for sleep apnea, my hope is that greater awareness of treatment options may encourage more people to get screened and seek treatment," she told Fox News Digital. Somers noted that the condition completely resolved in about 25% of participants without diabetes and 15% of those with type 2 diabetes. "This is a very exciting time in treating sleep apnea patients." The study’s findings do not mean patients should stop using CPAP or other prescribed treatments, the researchers emphasized. Additional research is needed to determine retatrutide's long-term safety and effectiveness for sleep apnea. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "There’s hope on the horizon," Somers said. "We have the CPAP, we have mandibular devices, we have postural therapy, where you try to avoid sleeping on your back, and now we’ve got drug therapies that can potentially not just reduce your apnea, but also make you sleep better ... and reduce the risk of future cardiovascular events."

articles.title: She took birth control for acne. It started ‘feeding’ a hidden cancer
articles.summary: Claudia Pereira didn't know starting birth control for adult acne would lead to a shocking, rare cancer diagnosis. She told USA TODAY her story.
articles.body:
Most people aren't grateful for their acne , but for Claudia Pereira, it was a "blessing in disguise."

After struggling with blemishes in adulthood, she decided to start birth control at 37 to try to reduce them. Little did she know it would lead to her discovering a cancer hiding in her uterus .

After starting the pills, Pereira started bleeding. And it didn't stop − for months.

She was used to regular periods , so the nonstop bleeding raised alarms. Her prescribing doctor said it could take a few months for her body to get used to the new medication. So, she waited.

After months four and five of continued bleeding, Pereira's worries reignited.

"I was like, 'OK, is this normal?' It was too much. I became anemic after six months," she told USA TODAY.

Then the bleeding transformed into a thick discharge that added to her concern, so she went to urgent care. From there, she was transferred to a hospital for imaging. Rounds of testing, including a transvaginal ultrasound and MRI, revealed a 7-centimeter mass.

While Pereira and her care team were hopeful that the mass was a benign fibroid − a common, noncancerous tumor − pathology revealed it was something much worse: uterine leiomyosarcoma , a rare cancer that developed in the smooth muscles of her uterus.

"I panicked. I froze. I started thinking about chemo, work, my life, what's going to happen," she recalled feeling after learning the diagnosis. "It was terrifying. I went from thinking it was a common gynecological issue to learning that it was a rare form of cancer."

Uterine leiomyosarcoma is a type of cancer that grows in the muscle layer of the uterus, Mayo Clinic explains .

Sarcomas, a type of cancer that develops in bone or soft tissue throughout the body, are rare − making up only 1% of all cancer, explained Dr. Gina D'Amato , a sarcoma medical oncologist with Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center, part of the University of Miami Health System, who helped treat Pereira.

Uterine sarcomas themselves are rare, making up about 5% of all uterine cancers , according to the American Cancer Society .

Given that Pereira was younger than 50 at the time of her diagnosis, her case was even more unusual, D'Amato told USA TODAY.

"Most uterine sarcomas happen in people over the age of 40. The average age at diagnosis is about 60 years old," the American Cancer Society notes.

Like certain breast cancers, uterine leiomyosarcoma can have estrogen or progesterone receptors, which can cause the cancer to grow with these hormones present.

Pereira's tumors tested positive for these receptors, which is why starting the birth control probably triggered the severe symptoms she experienced.

The estrogen released in Pereira's regular cycle could have already been "feeding" the cancer, D'Amato explained, then "really grew quickly" when the extra hormones were added with the medication.

"In her case, she wasn't on (the birth control) for very long. My thought is that she got actually lucky, so to speak, in that it maybe allowed (the cancer) to grow and be found," D'Amato added.

More research is needed to better understand this type of cancer.

Pereira's mass was removed and scans showed no evidence that the disease had spread elsewhere in her body. For extra reassurance, Pereira underwent a hysterectomy , in which her uterus, cervix and fallopian tubes were removed.

After all those organs were sent to pathology, "everything came back clean, so that was another worry (gone)," she said. "I was very relieved."

Pereira was lucky. Given the tumor's size, D'Amato said she was "at high risk that it was going to spread."

Had the tumor been found six months to a year later, the situation could have been "a lot worse" without such a good outcome, D'Amato added.

In July, Pereira celebrated a year being cancer-free. And she's been making the most of it, from traveling to Bali for her birthday to spending time at home with her family, whom she called her "strong support system" that made all the difference in her journey.

"I had a second chance of life, and since then, I've just been living harder," she said.

She hopes sharing her story will help spread awareness about this rare cancer and inspire others to listen to their body and advocate for themselves.

"Be brave. Don't overthink it," she said to those who may struggle to speak up about their health. "Don't hesitate. Listen to your body. Your body will always tell you when something's wrong. I'm living proof."

D'Amato also encourages patients to listen to their bodies and know their family history. Plus, when starting any medication, she encourages patients to monitor closely, with a doctor's guidance.

"If a doctor puts you on a medicine, you have to make sure that you have a follow-up with that doctor, I would say within a month," D'Amato suggests, to discuss any potential side effects.

Pereira remains thankful for those little bumps on her face: "Thank God for the acne."

"Who knows how long (the cancer) was there. If I hadn't had taken birth control, I would have never known," she said.

articles.title: 3 Types of Relationships Everyone Should Have for Better Wellbeing, According to Psychologist Adam Grant
articles.summary: When you have a problem, it’s natural to turn to the same friend or your partner to vent, whether you’re frustrated with work, a blunt text from a family member or the state of the world.
articles.body: When you have a problem, it’s natural to turn to the same friend or your partner to vent, whether you’re frustrated with work, a blunt text from a family member or the state of the world. But it’s important to foster different kinds of connections so you can have people you go to for different things, Adam Grant, Ph.D., organizational psychologist and author of the new book “Vibe,” tells TODAY.com. He recommends seeking out these three kinds of relationships to make sure you’re getting the range of outlets we all need. Mental Health Tip of the Day: The 3 Most Important Relationships to Build Connection Grant says his research points to three important types of connections based on studies of interactions and relationships from around the world. He came up with these terms based on patterns he noticed of common goals and interests. Companions: someone you can confide in and vice versaPals: someone you have fun withAllies: someone you’re helping pursue goals and vice versa Why It Matters “There’s actually some strong evidence showing that if you go to different friends for different things, you actually have higher well-being than people who go to one friend for everything,” Grant explains. “If you only have one person that you can count on to collaborate with, to enjoy and or confide in, then you’re at risk of basically overburdening that person and putting too much stress and pressure on the relationship,” he adds. “Whereas if you have a couple of pals that you could call when you’re bored, you have some companions that are great shoulders to cry on, you have some allies that you could do a project with, that allows you basically to have more sources of support available.” Grant says it’s beneficial to understand relationships in this way — as opposed to categorizing them by how close you are or how you know them — because “that doesn’t tell us anything about why we’re connected.” “What purpose does this relationship serve? What role do these people play in our life? I think that matters because if you’re not on the same page with people about what kind of bond you have or what kind you’re trying to build, it’s a recipe for disappointment and even sometimes feeling betrayed.” Research also shows that close friendships improve overall life satisfaction, protect against depression and reduce the likelihood of dying from all causes. How to Get Started The first thing to do when you’re forming a new connection with someone or reassessing an old one is deciding which of the three bonds you want it be, Grant says. Then you can decide a next step based on your choice. For example, for an ally, ask about a goal or challenge and try to help them. Pals should find a common interest, like karaoke or pickleball, and make plans around that activity. And with companions, try to get deep by talking about regrets, embarrassing moments or something along those lines, Grant suggests. And if it turns out you’re not on the same page about the connection you’re trying to build, rather than writing that person off entirely, you can instead think about how they could better fit into your life in another way, Grant adds.

articles.title: Study estimates 75% of NFL players who died over 15-year span had CTE
articles.summary: An estimated 75% of professional football players who died over a 15-year span had signs of chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE, a study published Wednesday found. It’s the highest estimation to date.
articles.body: An estimated 75% of professional football players who died over a 15-year span had signs of chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE, a study published Wednesday found. It’s the highest estimation to date. Most recently, a study published in August by the same group estimated that one-quarter of NFL players who died in a five-year span had CTE. The new study, published in JAMA Network Open, put the figure at three times higher. Not all people with signs of CTE in the brain go on to experience cognitive decline or dementia, and some people may never experience symptoms at all. A smaller proportion of the former players in the analysis were estimated to have dementia, about 27%, the study found. The results were surprising, said study leader Yorghos Tripodis, the director of statistics and data management at the Boston University Alzheimer’s Disease and CTE Center. Boston University houses the UNITE Brain Bank, which studies the effects of repetitive head trauma in donated brains, including the brains of athletes, military personnel and others. “I had to double-check the numbers,” Tripodis said. Still, he said, the number is a best guess. “Right now we don’t know how to diagnose CTE when people are alive, so we are trying to estimate.” In an emailed statement, an NFL spokesperson said, in part, that the league “continuously strives to make the game of football safer, including by implementing strategies to reduce concussions and head impacts.” Repeated blows and bias When a person’s head jolts during an impact, the brain — which is suspended in fluid inside the skull — can slam into the skull or twist, said Dr. Julian Bailes, chair of the neurosurgery department at Endeavor Health in the Chicago area. Each blow is an opportunity for proteins called tau to build up in the brain. “If that happens over and over again, that damage accrues,” said Bailes, who wasn’t involved with the new research. The disease can affect parts of the brain involved with regulating behavior and emotions, which can lead to memory loss, depression, violent mood swings and other symptoms. Those symptoms can also be linked to other illnesses. Although CTE can cause symptoms similar to those of other neurodegenerative diseases, such as dementia and Parkinson’s disease, the signature it leaves on the brain is unique, Bailes said. One huge hurdle in studying the prevalence of CTE is that the microscopic changes don’t show up on brain scans. That means the condition can be diagnosed only during an autopsy. Past research has been criticized for bias, since people with cognitive decline and their families are much likelier to either donate their brains to brain banks after they die or ask for autopsies — a previous study by Boston University researchers found that 99% of the brains donated to research by former NFL players had signs of CTE. In the new study, Tripodis and his team tried to remove as much of that bias as possible to determine a more accurate estimate of CTE rates in former NFL players. They combined data from the UNITE Brain Bank with national death records of other former NFL players who died from 2008 to 2023. In total, the researchers looked at data from 396 donated brains, plus information from 1,966 other deceased former NFL players. They factored in the ages of death along with estimated rates of mild cognitive impairment and dementia in former NFL players older than 50. About 93% of the donated brains had signs of CTE, which shows up as structural damage in the brain. The research team calculated that the families of players with symptoms of cognitive decline were about five times likelier to donate brains than the families of players without symptoms and then performed a statistical analysis to correct for that bias. From there, they estimated that among the roughly 2,360 former players who died during the 15-year time frame, about 1,760, or nearly 75%, had CTE. In comparison, only about 1% of brains donated to banks in the U.S., Austria and Brazil have signs of the disease, the researchers said. But plenty of people with signs of CTE never develop symptoms, Tripodis said. The researchers estimated that 27% of the 2,360 players studied had dementia. The dementia “can be from all causes,” Tripodis said. “But it is very likely that in this specific population that CTE is causing dementia.” Reducing impacts Until doctors figure out a way to diagnose CTE while people are still alive, any studies quantifying how many people have the condition will be estimations, said Dr. Jim Kelly, a professor emeritus of neurology at the University of Colorado Anschutz. “These are all estimates. They had no autopsies on five times as many players who died as they did have autopsies for,” said Kelly, who wasn’t involved in the research. Some of the autopsies may also have revealed just one or a couple of lesions associated with CTE, “and it seems unlikely that that would lead to anything in terms of a behavior change or dementia,” he said. Those are difficult studies to do, Bailes agreed. They seek to determine “how many people out there have a condition when not all of them are symptomatic,” he said, adding that the findings are a call for more research into diagnosing CTE in people who are still living. “If you can’t tell if someone has a certain disease until they’re dead, you really can’t help them,” he said. In the meantime, prevention is key, Tripodis said: “If you reduce the number of brain injuries, brain impacts, you substantially decrease the risk.” The NFL has already implemented measures to try to reduce the number of high-impact hits players face. They include redesigned helmets — such as the Guardian Cap — and the dynamic kickoff rule, which leads to lower collision speeds.

articles.title: The Simple High-Protein and Fiber Dinner Combo a Women’s Health Doctor Eats Every Night
articles.summary: No matter how much you meal prep, dinner can still be a challenge. Here, Dr. Jen Ashton shares her formula for filling weeknight meals with protein and fiber.
articles.body: No matter how dedicated you are to meal-prepping, there’s one question that can still catch you off-guard during a busy week: What’s for dinner? For Dr. Jennifer Ashton, an OB-GYN who is also board-certified in obesity medicine, the answer relies on a surprisingly simple formula for healthy, filling meals. She aims to get three specific nutrients in her dinners, which support heart health, bone health, gut health and more, she said during a Oct. 28 segment on the TODAY Show. The Perfect Combination for Filling Weeknight Dinners “The approach should be lean protein, fiber ... and a healthy fat,” Ashton said. We all need protein to build and maintain our bone and muscle health, TODAY.com explained previously. Protein also plays a huge role in regulating our hormones, and it supports the immune system. Protein is also digested more slowly than carbohydrates, so it can help keep you feeling full. Some examples of healthy, lean protein include chicken or turkey breast, fish, tofu, Greek yogurt or cottage cheese, beans and lentils. When it comes to fiber, Ashton recommends that people aim to get 30 grams per day, which can be a challenging goal to meet. “It’s hard to get that amount,” she said. “None of us are. So make sure that you’re loading up on the vegetables.” She prefers to steam or grill her veggies, which means she doesn’t need to add much fat during the cooking process. Not only does fiber have massive benefits for our gut health, but it also supports heart health, blood sugar levels and our hormonal health, Ashton explained previously. Look for high-fiber vegetables, like sweet potato, Brussels sprouts and broccoli. You can also find fiber in large amounts in fruit, (especially raspberries and pears), whole grains (like oats and bulgar wheat) as well as legumes, such as black beans and chickpeas. Finally, think about healthy fats, which support heart health and also help keep you feeling full. Ashton said she gravitates towards foods like avocado and olive oil to find healthy fats. As a bonus, avocado is also rich in fiber. With this combination of foods, Ashton doesn’t recommend people limit their portions at dinnertime. “If you eat intuitively and you eat (this combination of nutrients), you will stop eating when you’re full,” she said.

articles.title: RFK Jr. takes shortcut to make some peptides more widely available
articles.summary: The Department of Health and Human Services is giving compounding pharmacies a temporary green light to make six peptides while the agency continues to work on a formal rule change.
articles.body: The Department of Health and Human Services is giving compounding pharmacies a temporary green light to make six peptides while the agency continues to work on a formal rule change. In a notice filed Wednesday, the agency said it would exercise “enforcement discretion,” meaning it will not take legal action against compounding pharmacies that make the six unapproved peptides. In practice, that means these pharmacies can start offering them now, even though the peptides aren’t yet on the Food and Drug Administration’s list of ingredients compounding pharmacies are allowed to make. The six peptides are BPC-157, epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, semax and TB-500. They’ve been promoted online as treatments for everything from faster healing to younger-looking skin and a longer lifespan. None are approved by the FDA, and the agency’s own scientists concluded there is insufficient data to prove they are safe and effective. The FDA said compounding pharmacies must certify the identity and purity of the compounds. They must also now report side effects, which was not previously mandated. The move comes as a growing “gray market” has sprung up around peptides, where retailers sell them labeled “for research use only,” a legal workaround that lets them claim they aren’t meant for humans. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and others have argued that allowing peptides to be compounded would move people away from this gray market and toward safer products. “Under President Trump’s leadership, HHS is working to put prevention and patient safety at the center of health care—and that includes confronting the risks of black-market peptides,” Emily Hilliard, an HHS spokesperson, said in a statement. Dr. Peter Lurie, a former FDA official who now leads the Center for Science in the Public Interest watchdog group, said the FDA was essentially “turning a blind eye” to widen access to drugs that have not been proven to work. Compounding pharmacies generally may use only ingredients the FDA has added to an official list known as the bulk drugs substances list. Adding an ingredient requires the FDA to propose a rule, take public comment and issue a final rule, a process that can take several months. The agency took a step toward that process in July, when an FDA advisory panel narrowly voted in favor of adding six peptides to the bulk list. The panel included six new appointees with ties to the peptide industry and another who is the son of a U.S. representative who has pushed Kennedy to make peptides more available. (During that meeting, some committee members expressed concerns that the recommendation could make it harder for the FDA to say no to other unapproved drugs in the future.) On Tuesday and Wednesday, the FDA was scheduled to meet outside groups, including Medivant Healthcare, a compounding pharmacy that offers peptides, according to Reginfo.gov, a federal website that tracks government regulations. Shabbir Safdar, executive director of the Partnership for Safe Medicines, which researches the dangers of counterfeit medicines, said both the enforcement discretion and upcoming rule change would expose Americans to “untested dangerous substances.” “Imagine what it means for the nation’s top drug regulator to announce they won’t enforce the laws on people making completely untested compounds and distributing them to the public,” Safdar said.

articles.title: Shortfall of deceased donors: 20 years after father donates part of liver for son, mother gives hers for second transplant
articles.summary: Mumbai man undergoes second liver transplant as deceased donor shortage persists; 19 years after father donated, mother donates amid low cadaver donation rates in India.
articles.body: Mumbai: Nearly two decades after receiving a portion of his father’s liver as an 11-year-old due to a lack of deceased donors, a 30-year-old man has once again had to rely on a living family member for a second organ transplant. Top transplant specialists said on Wednesday that he has joined a small group of patients in the country to undergo a second liver transplant after living a long life with the first graft.This time his mother had to step forward as the donor. The organ donation rates and transplant infrastructure have improved over the last 19 years, rising from just 3 deceased donor liver transplants in 2007 to 34 by July of this year.But the numbers could not help Jitin Shirke, an Andheri resident who was placed on Zonal Transplant Coordination Centre (ZTCC) recipient list in mid-June. “My condition deteriorated within a couple of weeks of enlisting. I was unconscious for four days and doctors advised us that an immediate transplant was required,” Shirke said.Following an evaluation, his mother was deemed an eligible donor. Doctors at Jaslok Hospital, where the surgery took place, said that the patient suffered from autoimmune cirrhosis. They said that while graft failure typically occurs in the early post-transplant period, Shirke enjoyed 19 years of graft survival before his body ultimately faced late rejection.“Deceased organ donors are still less and very few patients are fortunate enough to find an eligible living donor in their immediate family on such short notice. This patient was lucky,” said Dr Aabha Nagral, a liver transplant specialist at the hospital who was involved in the case.About 80% of all organ transplants are from living donors like Jitin’s parents. According to data from Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, only 18% to 20% of transplants in India come from deceased donors. This is in contrast to developed nations, where deceased donors account for 85% to 95% of transplants.Jitin recalled that during his first transplant as a child, his family had to make the rounds of multiple hospitals because very few facilities had the necessary infrastructure at the time.Dr S K Mathur, who performed Jitin’s initial transplant in 2007 and now serves as president of ZTCC, said that India’s Transplantation of Human Organs Act was passed in 1994, a decade after similar legislation in the United States.“If we want to increase organ donation and transplant, there needs to be stricter auditing of hospitals. articles.title: Stroke cases more than double in two years: Govt data
articles.summary: Odisha stroke cases more than doubled from 4,252 in 2023-24 to 9,000+ in 2025-26, govt data shows; doctors urge treatment within 4.5 hours.
articles.body: Bhubaneswar: The number of stroke cases in Odisha has more than doubled in two years from 4,252 in 2023-24 to over 9,000 in 2025-26, as recorded by the state govt, raising concern among health experts ahead of World Stroke Day on Oct 29.Doctors attributed the rise to hypertension, diabetes, obesity, smoking, sedentary lifestyle, unhealthy dietary habits and genetic factors. They stressed the need for treatment within the critical four-and-a-half-hour “golden period” to improve the chances of recovery.The neurology department of SCB Medical College and Hospital, Cuttack, treats around 400 brain stroke patients annually, witnessing a steady rise in such cases. The scenario is no different at AIIMS Bhubaneswar.Professor in the neurology department of a private medical college, Dr Lulup Kumar Sahoo, said the theme of this year’s World Stroke Day, ‘Every Minute Counts’, underlines the importance of acting quickly when stroke symptoms appear.“If a person shows signs such as facial drooping, arm weakness, speech difficulty or sudden paralysis on one side of the body, they should be taken to the nearest hospital with CT scan facilities immediately. A general medicine doctor or a neurologist can manage the patient,” he said, adding his department treats at least 200 stroke patients every month. “The number is increasing every year due to changes in food habits and lifestyle, as well as hypertension and genetic factors. Several studies indicate that Odisha is reporting more stroke cases than the national average,” he said.He further said strokes are mainly of two types — ischaemic and haemorrhagic. An ischaemic stroke occurs when a blood clot blocks a vessel supplying blood to the brain, while a haemorrhagic stroke happens when a blood vessel in the brain bursts and causes bleeding. Both can damage the brain and lead to weakness, speech difficulty or paralysis, making early treatment crucial.Senior consultant in neurology, Dr Laxmidhar Parhi, said managing high blood pressure is essential. “Awareness of risk factors can help prevent stroke. The first four and a half hours after the onset of symptoms are critical, and timely treatment during this period can significantly improve recovery,” he said.An earlier study published in The Lancet Regional Health–Southeast Asia under the National Stroke Registry Programme of the Indian Council of Medical Research said rural residents of Cuttack face a lifetime stroke risk of nearly one in seven.The study, which analysed stroke incidence and mortality across five regions of India during 2018-19, found that stroke remains a major public health concern, particularly among rural populations. articles.title: Celtic fan left with bleeding on the brain in 'ferocious' attack after Old Firm derby
articles.summary: The 48-year-old victim was knocked to the ground as he was trying to board a Celtic supporters’ bus
articles.body:
Three men have been jailed for their parts in a "ferocious" assault which left a football fan with bleeding on the brain following the Scottish Cup quarter-final between Rangers and Celtic .

The attack took place outside Ibrox stadium in Glasgow on 8 March after Celtic won the match 4-2 on penalties.

Scott Dragsness, 55, and Ben Stanex, 24, both from Belfast, and Andrew Graham, 21, from Dundonald, had admitted carrying out the attack.

The Crown Office said the three men, all from Northern Ireland, knocked their 48-year-old victim to the ground as he was trying to board a Celtic supporters' bus.

They then proceeded to kick and stamp on his head and body with such ferocity that he was left lying unconscious in the road, the court heard.

They also shouted abuse at him relating to religion, with prosecutors telling the court the attack was a hate crime motivated by religious prejudice.

The man was taken to nearby Queen Elizabeth University Hospital, where scans revealed a bleed on the brain.

A police drone monitoring the dispersal of fans from Ibrox stadium captured the entirety of the attack, while a further recording was captured by a motorist stuck in traffic near the supporters' bus.

Dragsness, Stanex and Graham all pleaded guilty to a charge of assault to severe injury and danger of life at Glasgow Sheriff Court on 7 October.

At the same court on Wednesday, Dragsness was sentenced to 18 months' imprisonment while Stanex and Graham each received a 12-month sentence.

The three were also handed seven-year football banning orders, meaning they cannot enter any football ground in the UK or travel to support any team.

In his sentencing remarks published online, Sheriff Andrew McIntyre told the men they had each been involved in a "concerted act of serious violence".

"As part of the attack the complainer was punched and fell to the ground," he said.

"Whilst he was on the ground the attack continued and he was repeatedly kicked on the head and body and he was stamped upon.

"Such was the ferocity of the attack that he lost consciousness and was seriously injured.

"To inflict such violence on a person was an inherently dangerous act which posed an obvious danger of the complainer's life.

"To make matters worse, during the attack abuse relating to religion was shouted at the complainer."

The sheriff told the trio the custodial sentences were necessary to protect the public and act as a deterrent to similar offending.

He added that community sentences would be "inadequate" because they would "fail to reflect the seriousness of the crime or the community's disapproval (of) sectarian, football related violence".

Fraser Gibson of the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service, who is procurator fiscal for Glasgow and Strathkelvin, said: "Football-related violence is a blight on Scotland's communities. It will not be tolerated.

"The victim in this case was subjected to mindless sectarian thuggery by the three accused, who were visitors to the city.

"It should be understood that anyone who involves themselves in football-related disorder can expect to be held accountable by COPFS, Police Scotland and the courts using every tool available to us."

articles.title: Date-rape drug at center of Cornell sex assault allegations can leave victims unaware of surroundings
articles.summary: A former Cornell University student described feeling severe dissociation after taking ketamine before an alleged fraternity gang rape.
articles.body: An investigation into an alleged gang rape at a Cornell University fraternity has thrust the illicit use of ketamine into the spotlight, calling attention to the powerful anesthetic’s use on college campuses as a date-rape drug. The former Cornell student testified before the university’s hearing panel that ketamine made her feel "like her lights were on but no one was home," describing a state of "vague consciousness." During an Oct. 23 appearance on "Fox & Friends," Dr. Stephanie Widmer, a Fox News contributor and addiction specialist in New York, warned that the drug’s physiological effects can leave people unable to defend themselves or understand their environment. INSIDE EXPLOSIVE CORNELL RAPE ALLEGATIONS: 7 MEN ACCUSED, CONFLICTING ACCOUNTS AND A POLITICAL FIRESTORM "When you say the lights are on, but nobody’s home, that’s a pretty good way to describe it," Widmer said. "You can essentially have no awareness of your surroundings." Ketamine affects NMDA receptors in the brain and can alter vital signs, according to the doctor. "It can cause profound sedation, and it can cause dissociation, which is essentially the sensation of your brain not really being attached to your body," she said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES While ketamine has legitimate medical uses — it was used as a battlefield anesthetic during the Vietnam War and remains FDA-approved for general anesthesia — the drug is also abused recreationally at parties, raves and nightclubs. The Drug Enforcement Administration classifies ketamine as a Schedule III controlled substance and identifies it, alongside Rohypnol and GHB, as a drug that can be used to facilitate sexual assault. The agency says these substances can cause sedation, confusion and memory loss, leaving victims vulnerable. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP When asked why ketamine falls into the category of date-rape drugs, Widmer said it can affect both cognitive function and physical awareness. "There are a number of date-rape drugs that are out there, and ketamine does fall into that category because of what it can do to your sensorium," she added. Widmer also warned about mixing ketamine with alcohol or other substances, which can compound the drugs’ effects and increase the risk of dangerous sedation and respiratory depression. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "They’re combining them with other substances, they’re combining them with alcohol, and that can compound the effects of these drugs," she said. "It can cause really profound sedation. It can be incredibly dangerous." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Widmer said her biggest concern is how parents discuss the dangers of drugs with their children, especially before sending them off to college. "Everybody knows to say drugs are bad and not to do drugs, and you never know what you’re getting, but really understanding what some of these drugs can do is really important... that they’re not benign and that they can cause dissociation."

articles.title: Newport mum of critically ill baby denied food at Grange Hospital
articles.summary: Sophie Price had given birth in the same hospital five days earlier but was denied a hot meal.
articles.body:
A first-time mum was denied hospital meals while her baby was "fighting for her life" because she was not breastfeeding.

Sophie Price, 22, was "shocked" when staff refused to give her a meal while her daughter Florence was being treated on a paediatric ward at Grange University Hospital in Cwmbran, Torfaen.

Despite giving birth in the hospital five days earlier, she was told she was no longer classed as a patient as she was not breastfeeding, so she would not be provided with meals.

Aneurin Bevan health board said it was "sorry to hear about Sophie's experience" and was "committed to supporting families throughout their child's stay".

"It was just an awful experience. I just needed a hot meal to keep going for my daughter," said Sophie, from Newport.

Her family said they spent more than £1,000 on food from the canteen and takeaway meals during their three-week stay at the hospital while Florence was treated.

Sophie had only left the hospital - which earlier this week denied online claims it was "dangerous" and "dreadful" - for 24 hours before she and her husband Ryli Price had to return when they realised Florence was not able to breathe and the "colour started to drain from her".

"Florence started to make some really harsh grunting sounds, it sounded like a death rattle coming from her chest up into her mouth," she said.

Sophie ran into the A&E department screaming "she's not breathing" and credited the quick response of medical staff who helped save her daughter's life.

Florence was diagnosed with bronchiolitis , rhinoviruses - which causes the common cold - and a blood infection, which meant her lungs could not operate on their own.

She was placed on a machine that pumped air into her lungs via a mask.

Sophie said despite being "hungry and exhausted" she was denied a meal while her daughter was "in intensive care fighting for her life".

"Imagine being in a hospital with your seriously ill baby on breathing support monitors, overwhelmed with worry, anxiety and stress, only to be told you aren't entitled to a meal because you're formula feeding instead of breastfeeding," she said.

Sophie said she was bleeding through her clothes and "in a lot of pain" as her hips had to be put back in place after being dislocated during childbirth.

She also had a build-up of fluid in her feet called oedema , adding: "My feet, they were the size of elephant trunks to the point where I couldn't even walk from the one corridor to the next."

Sophie said she and Ryli were told Florence may need to be induced into a coma at any point and it was "so touch-and-go the whole time".

At one point, Sophie said she realised she had not eaten for about 28 hours and remembered seeing a food trolley being brought round to mums on the ward.

She said: "I remember them saying to me 'oh hi mum, hope you're OK, are you hungry?' And me saying 'oh yeah, I'm absolutely starving, I haven't eaten in ages. What have you got'?'"

Sophie was asked if she was breastfeeding, which she had not been able to do after the first 24 hours of Florence's life as she was no longer taking to her breast milk.

She explained this to staff and said Florence was being given formula, only to be told she was not able to have any food

"I remember just being so shocked. It was so horrific," Sophie said, adding she already felt "disappointed" at being unable to breastfeed.

Due to her husband's paternity leave coming to an end, Sophie said she had "never been in such a vulnerable situation" and relied on family members to finish work and bring her food while she stayed at Florence's bedside.

Mothers are provided meals while under the care of hospital maternity services as both them and their baby are classed as patients, whether they are breastfeeding or not.

On paediatric wards only the child is classed as the patient, but the hospital's policy is to provide breastfeeding mums with meals as this directly supports the baby's feeding and nutrition.

For babies who are formula-fed, the health board said formula was "provided as needed" by the hospital, but Sophie said she was told she would need to bring it in herself.

Sophie's mother contacted the hospital about the issue, so it continued providing formula for Florence.

Sophie called the policy "outdated" and said it discriminated against formula-feeding mothers "who are doing their very best in difficult circumstances".

She thinks all hospitals should provide meals for mothers, regardless of how they are feeding their babies.

The health board thanked Sophie for her feedback and said it understood "how difficult and stressful it can be for parents when their child is in hospital".

It added: "Where parents are unable to access the hospital canteen, have limited support, or are unable to leave their child's bedside, ward teams can provide a selection of basic food items and refreshments to help meet immediate needs.

"Parents can also access a discounted hospital meal through a ward voucher scheme and where a family is experiencing financial hardship, support can be discussed with the ward team.

"Requests are considered on a case-by-case basis to ensure help is provided fairly and appropriately, taking account of the family's circumstances and the needs of the child."

articles.title: Mulher que desapareceu durante internação em Curitiba é encontrada | G1
articles.standfirst: Roseli Mendes, de 60 anos, faz tratamento oncológico e estava internada. Ela foi localizada após uma pessoa reconhecer a mulher em reportagem e avisar a família. Hospital continua apurando o caso.
articles.summary: Roseli Mendes, de 60 anos, faz tratamento oncológico e estava internada. Ela foi localizada após uma pessoa reconhecer a mulher em reportagem e avisar a família. Hospital continua
articles.body:
Roseli Mendes, de 60 anos, que desapareceu enquanto estava internada no Hospital Santa Casa, em Curitiba , foi encontrada por volta das 23h de quarta-feira (28), em um terminal de ônibus em Pinhais, na Região Metropolitana de Curitiba (RMC).

Segundo a filha, Camila Mendes, uma pessoa reconheceu Roseli após assistir à reportagem, entrou em contato com a família e informou onde ela estava. No momento em que foi encontrada, a paciente estava desorientada.

“Graças a Deus. Ela foi encontrada. Foi mostrada na reportagem, a pessoa viu, me ligou e, no momento, ela estava no terminal, desorientada”, contou Camila.

A filha agradeceu à pessoa que localizou a mãe, à equipe de reportagem e à Polícia Militar, que ajudou nas buscas.

Roseli Mendes, de 60 anos, desapareceu enquanto estava internada no Hospital Santa Casa — Foto: Arquivo familiar

Roseli faz tratamento contra um câncer e havia passado por uma sessão de radioterapia cerca de dez dias antes de desaparecer. Segundo a filha, desde domingo (25), a paciente apresentava sinais de alucinações.

A família levou Roseli ao Hospital Santa Casa na noite de segunda-feira (26). Após identificar um quadro de inflamação no pulmão, a equipe médica determinou a internação para que ela recebesse medicação. A internação ocorreu na terça-feira (27), por volta das 18h.

Na manhã de quarta-feira (28), Camila voltou ao hospital para levar roupas e objetos pessoais para a mãe, mas não a encontrou no quarto.

Ao perguntar às outras pacientes que dividiam o quarto com Roseli, a filha foi informada de que a mãe havia dito que iria embora e saído do local. Segundo os relatos, ela deixou o hospital com um acesso venoso no braço e usando a pulseira de identificação da instituição.

A família passou a procurar a paciente nas imediações do hospital e em outros locais da cidade. Camila também procurou uma delegacia e o Instituto Médico-Legal (IML), mas não conseguiu informações sobre o paradeiro da mãe.

Após ser encontrada, Roseli voltou à Santa Casa, onde permanece em segurança, recebendo atendimento médico e sendo monitorada. Segundo Camila, a equipe médica deve realizar exames para investigar o quadro de saúde da paciente, incluindo possíveis inflamações no pulmão e na cabeça.

“Foi um desespero, muito angustiante. Eu fiquei o tempo todo aqui no hospital esperando notícias. Ela ainda está meio perdida, viveu um momento estranho, mas está desorientada e cansada. Vão fazer exames para ver”, relatou.

Em nota divulgada nesta quinta-feira (29), o Hospital Santa Casa de Curitiba comemorou o reencontro e informou que continua apurando as circunstâncias do caso em conjunto com as autoridades. Leia na íntegra:

"A ISCMC e a Santa Casa de Curitiba ficaram felizes com o desfecho positivo do reencontro da paciente. Desde os primeiros momentos de ontem, não deixaram de se esmerar na busca, no fornecimento de amparo aos familiares, na análise da situação e na prestação de informações aos envolvidos e, principalmente, às autoridades. Hoje, 29/10/2026, a paciente encontra-se em segurança na instituição, recebendo atendimento médico e sendo monitorada. Continuamos com os procedimentos de verificação e apuração no hospital, em conjunto com as autoridades".

articles.title: Batida entre carretas deixa motorista morto na BR-262, em MG  | G1
articles.standfirst: Motorista de 45 anos perdeu o controle da direção após uma falha mecânica no veículo e invadiu a contramão. O acidente ocorreu em Luz, no Centro-Oeste de Minas, na quarta-feira (28).
articles.summary: Motorista de 45 anos perdeu o controle da direção após uma falha mecânica no veículo e invadiu a contramão. O acidente ocorreu em Luz, no Centro-Oeste de Minas, na quarta (28).
articles.body:
Batida entre carretas causa morte de motorista, em Luz — Foto: PRF/Divulgação

Um homem de 45 anos morreu e outras duas pessoas ficaram feridas em uma batida de frente entre duas carretas na BR-262, na Serra de Luz , na quarta-feira (28). O trecho ficou totalmente interditado até o início da noite, e o congestionamento chegou a 11 quilômetros.

De acordo com a Polícia Rodoviária Federal (PRF), a carreta bitrem estava descendo a Serra de Luz, quando teria apresentado uma pane no sistema de freios. O motorista perdeu o controle da direção, invadiu a pista contrária e bateu de frente com a outra carreta, que seguia na direção contrária.

O motorista da carreta, de 45 anos, natural de Linhares (ES), morreu no local. A perícia da Polícia Civil foi chamada para os trabalhos de investigação. Em seguida, o corpo da vítima foi encaminhado para o o Instituto Médico Legal (IML) de Luz.

No bitrem, estavam o motorista de 25 anos, e a passageira, de 28 anos, ambos naturais de Catalão (GO). Os dois ficaram feridos e foram encaminhados ao Hospital de Luz.

O bitrem estava carregado com milho a granel e a carreta transportava sprays de inseticidas.

Após a liberação da pista, equipes da concessionária responsável pelo trecho atuaram na limpeza da pista e na remoção dos veículos para a liberação definitiva da via.

articles.title: Porsche: Júri de Fernando Sastre entra no segundo dia; amigo e ex-namorada confirmaram que ele bebeu | G1
articles.standfirst: No total, 14 testemunhas serão ouvidas. Fernando Sastre é acusado de matar o motorista de aplicativo Ornaldo da Silva Viana em acidente na Avenida Salim Farah Maluf, em março de 2024. Defesa sustenta que houve homicídio culposo, sem intenção de matar.
articles.summary: No total, 14 testemunhas serão ouvidas. Fernando Sastre é acusado de matar o motorista de aplicativo Ornaldo da Silva Viana em acidente na Avenida Salim Farah Maluf, em março de 2024. Defesa sustenta que houve homicídio culposo, sem intenção de matar.
articles.body:
O empresário Fernando Sastre, que matou o motorista de aplicativo Ornaldo da Silva Viana. — Foto: Reprodução

O julgamento do empresário Fernando Sastre de Andrade Filho, dono do Porsche azul, acusado de matar o motorista de aplicativo Ornaldo da Silva Viana, na Zona Leste de São Paulo — em 31 de março de 2024 — entra em seu segundo dia nesta quinta-feira (29).

O júri começou na quarta-feira (28) e no total 14 testemunhas testemunhas. O Ministério Público (MP) quer que o réu seja condenado a uma pena de mais de 20 anos de prisão.

O júri popular acontece no Fórum Criminal da Barra Funda, na Zona Oeste da capital. O MP acusa Fernando de dirigir embriagado o Porsche e bater o carro esportivo de luxo a 136 km/h na traseira do Renault Sandero da vítima, na Avenida Salim Farah Maluf, no Tatuapé. O limite da via é de 50 km/h.

Neste segundo dia de júri, devem ser ouvidos a policial militar que liberou Sastre, e o assistente técnico da defesa e da acusação, contratado para analisar provas periciais, elaborar pareceres e auxiliar na tese técnica. Depois, começa a fase de interrogatório do réu e, por fim, os debates.

Quatro pessoas foram ouvidas nesta quarta-feira (28), no primeiro dia do julgamento de Fernando Sastre, que dirigia um carro de luxo em alta velocidade na Avenida Salim Farah Maluf e matou o motorista de aplicativo Ornaldo da Silva Viana na madrugada de 31 de março de 2024.

Testemunhas confirmaram que Sastre havia consumido bebida alcoólica antes de dirigir. O filho da vítima relatou as dificuldades financeiras e psicológicas enfrentadas pela família após a morte do pai.

O primeiro a prestar depoimento foi Marcus Vinícius Rocha, amigo de Fernando, que estava no carro no momento do acidente. Ele foi ouvido como testemunha e vítima, porque também se machucou na colisão.

Marcus confirmou que Fernando estava alterado por causa da bebida. Ele também afirmou que foi com o amigo no carro porque não queria deixá-lo sozinho.

O depoimento seguinte foi o de Lucas, filho de Ornaldo. Ele contou sobre os problemas psicológicos e financeiros enfrentados por ele, pela mãe e pelos dois irmãos após a morte do pai.

Segundo o relato, a família chegou a receber cestas básicas de parentes e de uma igreja evangélica. Os familiares ainda são cobrados pelo banco, porque o carro de Ornaldo era financiado.

Deois, por videoconferência, foi a vez ex-namorada de Marcus. Ela também confirmou que Fernando havia bebido e estava cambaleante antes de dirigir.

A promotoria pede a condenação de Fernando Sastre a 20 anos de prisão. O julgamento deve terminar nesta quinta. A defesa de Fernando Sastre sustenta que houve homicídio culposo, quando não há intenção de matar.

Acidente matou motorista de aplicativo e feriu passageiro

Ornaldo da Silva Viana, de 52 anos, morreu depois que o Renault Sandero que dirigia foi atingido na traseira pelo Porsche conduzido por Fernando, na madrugada de 31 de março de 2024.

A batida ocorreu na Avenida Salim Farah Maluf, na Zona Leste de São Paulo, e foi registrada por câmeras de segurança (veja imagem acima).

Segundo a acusação, Fernando dirigia após consumir bebida alcoólica e em velocidade muito acima do limite da via. Laudo do Instituto de Criminalística apontou que o Porsche estava a cerca de 136 km/h no momento do impacto, em um trecho com limite de 50 km/h.

Ornaldo foi socorrido e levado ao Hospital Municipal do Tatuapé, mas não resistiu. O filho dele, Luam Silva, escreveu nas redes sociais: “Um sentimento de injustiça gigantesco dentro de mim”. Ele também pediu que a Justiça fosse feita.

Fernando deixou o local da batida e se apresentou à polícia no dia seguinte. Ele está preso preventivamente desde 6 de maio de 2024.

Jonas Marzagão, advogado de Fernando, diz que seu cliente é o único motorista envolvido em um acidente com morte que segue preso em São Paulo.

"Todos os reús nos casos similares estão respondendo em liberdade, inclusive com teste de bafômetro comprovando o uso do bebida alcoólica, e fuga do local de acidente. O que não aconteceu no caso de Fernando. Ele não fez o bafômetro na ocasião porque a polícia não tinha o aparelho para fazer no momento", falou Marzagão.

"Fernando não pediu socorro porque outras pessoas haviam telefonado e pedido, enquanto era retirado do carro. Mas ele ainda permaneceu no local do acidente até ser liberado pelas autoridades", completou o advogado.

articles.title: Pacientes de clínica de estética tentam reaver dinheiro | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo a Decon, mais de 40 denúncias relacionadas à Clínica Celita Toledo foram registradas. Local foi alvo de operação no dia 21 de outubro, após denúncias de três mortes.
articles.summary: Polícia Civil recebeu novas denúncias de pacientes que relatam problemas após cirurgias na Clínica Celita Toledo, em Laranjeiras, na Zona Sul do Rio.
articles.body:
A Polícia Civil recebeu novas denúncias de pacientes que relatam problemas após cirurgias na Clínica Celita Toledo, em Laranjeiras, na Zona Sul do Rio. O centro cirúrgico do estabelecimento foi interditado após denúncias envolvendo três mortes.

Segundo a Delegacia do Consumidor (Decon), mais de 40 denúncias relacionadas à clínica foram registradas. Além de pacientes que afirmam ter sofrido complicações após procedimentos, há relatos de pessoas que tiveram cirurgias canceladas e dizem não conseguir recuperar os valores pagos.

“O que era para ser um sonho acaba em pesadelo. Eu trabalhei muito para conseguir esse dinheiro para fazer essa cirurgia, eu não me sinto mais segura para operar com uma equipe que está sendo investigada, estou com meu emocional muito abalado. Eu só quero meu dinheiro de volta, mais nada”, disse uma paciente.

Fachada da Clínica Celita Toledo, em Laranjeiras, na Zona Sul do Rio — Foto: Reprodução/ TV Globo

A família da paciente Anna Clara dos Santos Lima afirma que ela teve complicações depois de passar por uma cirurgia. A jovem está internada no Hospital Municipal Ernesto Che Guevara, em Maricá, e deve passar por uma transfusão de sangue nos próximos dias.

“Ela passou por consulta com um médico, depois apareceu um segundo médico para operá-la e, depois, apareceu um terceiro médico. Às 4h da manhã terminou a operação e ela receberia alta às 11h no mesmo dia. Ela chegou em casa e a minha filha teve uma hemorragia pelo dreno, perdeu a consciência”, contou Marcelli Santos, mãe de Anna Clara.

Segundo a família, a paciente está se recuperando após receber atendimento médico.

“Eu falei com ele que ela teve uma hemorragia e ele disse que ela não perdeu sangue na cirurgia. Depois, ele falou que ela precisava de uma transfusão de sangue. A minha filha viu a morte de perto. Única coisa que a gente quer agora é a justiça e trazê-la para casa”, completou Marcelli.

Outras pacientes também relatam complicações após procedimentos realizados na clínica. Uma mulher, que pediu para não ser identificada, afirmou que precisará passar por uma cirurgia reparadora.

“Fiz a minha cirurgia no dia 6 de maio. O meu peito, eu estou com dupla bolha, dois peitos. Fui em outro lugar que apresentou um orçamento de R$ 38 mil para poder pagar um reparo. Pagar por um erro que não foi meu”, disse.

Anna Clara está internada no Hospital Municipal Ernesto Che Guevara, em Maricá, na Região dos Lagos — Foto: Reprodução/ TV Globo

Pacientes que pagaram por cirurgias que não foram realizadas afirmam que estão enfrentando dificuldades para receber o dinheiro de volta.

Uma delas diz ter pago R$ 7 mil e desistido do procedimento após os casos envolvendo a clínica.

“Mediante a tantos casos de mulheres mortas e vítimas desse grupo, eu estou com medo de operar. Já paguei R$ 7 mil e só quero meu dinheiro de volta. Eles querem obrigar a gente a operar porque eles alegam que estão operando em outra clínica. Mas eu não tenho mais coragem para operar. E ela alega que vai cobrar os 20%, né? Do valor da cirurgia”, afirmou.

Outra paciente disse que pagou R$ 14 mil por uma mastopexia com prótese, mas teve o procedimento cancelado após a interdição do centro cirúrgico.

“A menina do financeiro entrou no nosso quarto falando que as cirurgias tinham sido canceladas porque o centro cirúrgico tinha sido interditado. Sigo na minha luta para receber o meu dinheiro, porque foi R$ 14 mil que eu paguei numa mastopexia com prótese”, contou.

Material recolhido por policiais em operação na Clínica Celita Toledo — Foto: Reprodução/ TV Globo

A Polícia Civil realizou uma operação na Clínica Celita Toledo no dia 21 de outubro. O centro cirúrgico foi interditado após denúncias envolvendo três mortes. Pacientes também afirmam ter ficado com deformações após procedimentos realizados no local.

Durante a ação, os agentes encontraram medicamentos vencidos na clínica.

A polícia acredita que o número de pessoas que tiveram problemas relacionados ao estabelecimento possa ser maior.

A TV Globo procurou a Clínica Celita Toledo, que não se manifestou até a última atualização desta reportagem.

A Polícia Civil informou que apura as denúncias e analisa informações que possam contribuir para o esclarecimento dos fatos e para uma eventual responsabilização dos envolvidos.

articles.title: World Stroke Day: Five lifestyle habits to support better brain health
articles.summary: The brain is the center of human activity. Every thought, decision, emotion and action involves the brain.
articles.body: The brain is the center of human activity. Every thought, decision, emotion and action involves the brain. Yet we spend so much time planning our work, finances and responsibilities, while rarely giving the same attention to the way we live each day.On World Stroke Day, WE would encourage everyone to think about their daily habits. Taking care of the brain is not something we should remember only when a health problem arises. There are simple things we can practice every day that bring more discipline, clarity and balance into our lives.1. Begin every day with meditation and clarityEvery morning, spend some time meditating on life. What needs to be done today? What do you wish to achieve? Where are you going in life?Without some planning, we often end up doing whatever the day demands. One activity leads to another, somebody calls, something unexpected happens, and before we realize it, the entire day has passed.We always encourage people to spend ten to fifteen minutes in quiet reflection. Sit comfortably, allow the mind to settle and think about what deserves your attention.Meditation helps us become more attentive to our thoughts. Beginning the morning with a clear mind can make a difference to how we approach the rest of the day.2. Develop the habit of writing things downWhatever needs to be done, write it down.It may concern your work, your family, your health or something you have wanted to achieve for a long time. Make a habit of putting these thoughts on paper.When everything remains in the mind, it is easy to forget something or become occupied with too many things at once.Writing gives us an opportunity to look at our responsibilities properly. We can see what needs immediate attention, what can wait and what we should be working towards.It is a very simple habit, but one that can bring considerable order into daily life.3. Remember that life is meant to be livedLife is meant to be lived, experienced and enjoyed.We cannot spend our entire lives working, collecting responsibilities and carrying tension from one day into the next. What are we working towards if we never make time to enjoy what life offers?Make arrangements for good living. Spend time with good people. Maintain friendships, build meaningful relationships, visit beautiful places and travel whenever you have the opportunity.There is so much to experience in life. A conversation with a friend, a journey with family or a visit to a place you have never seen can bring happiness into an otherwise ordinary week.Our professional responsibilities are important, but personal happiness and relationships also deserve our time.4. Make physical activity a daily commitmentThe human body needs movement. Practice Yoga, go running, swimming or walking. Play a sport you enjoy. Choose something that encourages you to remain physically active.When someone begins learning a sport, notice how their attention changes. They think about improving their performance, preparing for the next session and learning something new.The mind has something interesting to engage with, while the body receives the exercise it needs.Regular physical activity is also important for cardiovascular health. It can help manage blood pressure, which is one of the major risk factors for stroke.Choose an activity that suits your health and physical capacity. Prepare properly before exercise and make it a regular part of your life.5. Learn the art of remaining calmOne of the most valuable things we can learn is how to remain calm.Imagine a river after heavy rainfall. The water is flowing violently, carrying mud and everything that comes in its way. It becomes difficult to approach or make use of that water.Now think of the same river when the flow has settled.Our mind can be much the same. When we are constantly angry, anxious or reacting to every small situation, we find it difficult to enjoy even the simplest things.We should learn to give the mind some quiet time.Look at a flower. Spend a few minutes in nature. Sit peacefully without feeling that something must always be done.There is a great deal of happiness in ordinary experiences when the mind is calm enough to appreciate them.These five habits do not require complicated arrangements. They can become part of the way we live every day.Along with these practices, proper nutrition, adequate sleep, blood pressure monitoring and regular medical care remain important for protecting long-term health. Anyone experiencing sudden facial weakness, arm weakness or difficulty speaking should seek emergency medical attention immediately.On World Stroke Day, let us remember that caring for the brain also means paying attention to our daily routine.A healthier life begins with the discipline of how each day is lived.Himalayan Siddhaa Akshar - Yoga Guru, Spiritual Leader, Author, Columnist, Founder: Akshar Yoga KendraaGet the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. articles.title: Science reveals why the brain connects to the opposite side of the body
articles.summary: Human brain is strange, and so are the mysteries related to it.
articles.body: Human brain is strange, and so are the mysteries related to it. As per a recent report published in the journal of News Medical Lifesciences, it was mentioned that the left side of the human brain controls the opposite side of your body, and the right side of your brain controls the left side of your body. Interestingly, this arrangement is not so obvious; this is because each side of your brain is linked to the side of your body, and the wiring would be simpler and less likely to fail. This crossed wiring is found even in almost all animals, even in simple nematode worms. A new analysis mentioned in the journal of Frontiers in Neuroanatomy by researchers Daniel Wang and Martin Wessendorf gives an idea of how this strange setup may have evolved.A question scientists have asked for centuriesThere’s no denying that this debate and curiosity around it is pretty old. After many centuries scientists still do not have a final answer. This new hypothesis builds on anatomical studies and offers a simple explanation. As per the study, Wessendorf, a neuroscientist and associate professor emeritus at the University of Minnesota, studies how the brainstem controls the cord. He and his co-author suggest that this crossed wiring started with a specific ancient visual system. In animals each eye sends sight information to the opposite side of the brain's optic tectum, a part of the brain that processes sight. The researchers think that once this side visual map was in place early in evolution, other systems used it as a template. As the study explains, adding touch, hearing, and movement circuits around an existing opposite-side map likely needed fewer changes than building a new same-side arrangement from scratch. In words, evolution chose the easier route, reusing an existing crossed wiring instead of creating a new one.Not the same as left-right brain specializationWell, it is important to explain that crossed wiring is not the same as right brain specialization. The researchers clarify that this phenomenon is different from lateralization, the type of left-right specialization that explains handedness. Crossed wiring is broad and symmetrical; each hemisphere of the brain simply connects to the side of the body, not to a special task.Why this arrangement might actually be smarterOther researchers propose that crossed wiring may actually lower wiring mistakes during brain growth. Theoretical work in the journal The Naked Scientists mentioned that a developing brain may be more likely to wire when one hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body instead of the same side. This might be because it gives a reliable developmental map for the nervous system. In fact, the researchers admit that this idea is still a hypothesis based on comparing anatomy across animals not on direct experiments or fossils. The next step, the paper says, is to test whether anatomical studies and fossil records back this optic tectum idea.Why this still mattersEven if a final answer is not yet reached, this research gives a part of the puzzle. It suggests that one of the brain's strangest design choices may not be random.
