articles.title: The hospital accordion player who has been busking for 35 years
articles.summary: Volunteer John Jones, 84, has been entertaining patients and visitors with his musical talents.
articles.body:
For 35 years, volunteer John Jones has been entertaining patients and visitors at Macclesfield District General Hospital by playing the accordion.

The 84-year-old retired engineer discovered his love of the accordion as a child, watching his father play the instrument.

"My dad played the accordion all the time and I could play the piano a little bit," he said.

"When he died, I started messing around with his accordion.

"One half is like a piano, but the other half is completely different with buttons.

"I had to teach myself, but I really enjoyed it."

He has since been using his musical talents to raise money for East Cheshire NHS Charity.

John's volunteering began after visiting the hospital with his mother-in-law in 1991 where he saw an appeal for a CT scanner.

He has since raised hundreds of thousands of pounds for the charity.

"One of the nicest moments was about five years after helping to raise the money for the scanner, I had to have a CT scan myself," said John who has an MBE for services to charity.

"The nurse said, 'That's ironic, you're using the scanner you helped pay for.' That really stayed with me."

The money has been used to fund a family room at the hospital intensive care unit, where his wife June died from sepsis in 2020.

"She'd been in intensive care five years earlier with sepsis as well, but she managed to survive that one," said John, who also performs in care homes.

"I asked if I could specifically collect for intensive care unit which is very close to my heart really because my youngest daughter is matron in intensive care in Australia.

"Obviously I know all the staff personally because they've been here all that time."

Zara Jones, chief executive at East Cheshire NHS Trust, said: "It's a privilege having so many people who are willing to give up their time to work here.

"A number of the volunteers I've met also have their own stories about care they've received here or their family or friends have had care here as well so it means a lot to them personally and we're really keen to support them."

articles.title: Warning signs that your adult child may be quietly cutting you off
articles.summary: Family estrangement experts reveal the subtle warning signs, from skipped holidays to shifted tone, that may precede a no-contact situation.
articles.body: Amid a growing trend of parent-child estrangement, experts say recognizing the early warning signs may help families address problems before they escalate into a no-contact situation. Nearly four in 10 Americans are currently estranged from at least one close family member, according to a 2025 YouGov poll of 4,395 U.S. adults. That includes 24% who reported estrangement from a sibling, 16% from a parent and 10% from a child. While estrangement can sometimes seem sudden, experts say subtle changes may signal that a family relationship is beginning to unravel. CUT OFF BY YOUR ADULT CHILD? PSYCHOLOGY RESEARCHER REVEALS WHAT PARENTS SHOULD DO NEXT The quiet signs Mary McLaughlin, a licensed couples and family therapist in Vienna, Virginia, said early signs may include an adult child becoming less willing to share details of their life directly with a parent. "You might find out about the trip, the new relationship or a promotion at work at the same time everyone else does," she told Fox News Digital. The parent may still be in contact with the adult child, McLaughlin said, but the child no longer chooses to share parts of their life directly. ADULT CHILDREN CUTTING OFF PARENTS AS SOME BLAME THERAPY FOR FAMILY ESTRANGEMENTS Other potential warning signs may include skipping family holidays, birthdays or weddings; leaving texts and calls unanswered; and reducing communication to brief or sporadic exchanges, according to the expert. The distance may become so noticeable that siblings, grandparents or other relatives comment that they have not seen or heard from the adult child in a long time. A child who once readily joined family photos but begins stepping out of them may also be signaling that they are starting to see themselves as separate from the family, McLaughlin said. Blythe Landry, a Pennsylvania-based therapist and founder of Blythe Landry Coaching, said other early signs may include a child becoming involved with a new social group that encourages estrangement over difficult conversations, or "beginning to rewrite history in a way that seems more damaging than what might have happened." The adult child may also become less willing to let a parent spend time with their grandchildren. ‘QUIET QUITTING’ IN MARRIAGE: THE SUBTLE SIGNS A SPOUSE HAS EMOTIONALLY CHECKED OUT The most telling sign may be a noticeable shift in the tone of the relationship, Landry said. "You know your child, and you know when the energy has shifted in a direction that seems dramatically harsher than in previous interactions." The shift to independence Laura Wellington, a Connecticut mother who has been estranged from her adult daughter since 2024, said it can be challenging to distinguish early signs of estrangement from typical moves toward independence. "It’s confusing to the parent because, a lot of times, they look like the general signs of a teenager moving into the young-adult zone — just pulling away and going off and establishing their lives," she told Fox News Digital. "That’s what I think confuses many parents, because they want to give them the space to start pulling away and showing signs of their own individuality and carving their path." "They don’t want to fight every battle, because if they fight every battle, then communication breaks down. So they try to pick and choose." Loss of respect One warning sign, according to Wellington, is if the child has an "I know everything, you know nothing" mindset. "What's happening in our society today is … a lot of ‘I know everything, you know nothing’ toward the parent," she said. "There's no respect for what the parents experience. There's no tolerance for them speaking up and saying, ‘No, this is not what you should be doing.’" "A lot of times, they look like the general signs of a teenager moving into the young-adult zone." In some cases, the child may begin treating the parent as a subordinate, according to Wellington. Some parents begin to notice a shift when their adult children start treating them with disrespect, pushing back on their opinions and positioning themselves as the authority in the relationship, she said. "They become the authority; they flip it. Anytime you say something, you’ll see them bark at the parent and push back on the parent. They really have no respect for the parent." Different worldviews Wellington also pointed to major differences in political, religious or lifestyle beliefs as a possible source of growing distance between parents and adult children. She suggested that some young people who become estranged are "more liberal in thinking," while acknowledging that the dynamic can also work in the opposite direction when a parent holds especially strong ideological views. "There is extremism sometimes where the parent is extremely something, and then the child … goes the other way," she said. Richard Blake, Ph.D., a Texas-based psychology researcher who focuses on anxiety and family estrangement, said an adult child’s unwillingness to consider differing views may signal trouble. He suggested that personality may play a role, with more argumentative adult children who are less willing to consider differing views potentially more prone to family estrangement. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Repeated cutoffs Another possible warning sign, according to Blake, is if the adult child has begun cutting off other people. He said parents should take note if an adult child has repeatedly stopped speaking to relatives or openly boasts about ending relationships. "Chances are, they're going to cut off someone else, and it may be the parent," he said. "If you haven’t been cut off yet, you may be in the firing line there." Communication breakdown Ongoing communication problems may be an early warning sign, Blake said, particularly when an adult child feels that a parent refuses to listen or acknowledge the child’s point of view. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "They may say, 'My parents just don’t listen. I cannot get through to them. It’s like talking to a brick wall.'" Parents who consistently dismiss their children’s concerns should not be surprised when conflict develops, he said. "If you don’t listen to your child, then don’t be surprised if you have conflict with them." Blake recommends listening actively, avoiding interruptions, repeating back what the other person has said and asking a simple follow-up question: "First, you say, 'Is there more?'" No clear warning While there may be some early signs, Blake emphasized that estrangement can sometimes appear suddenly, with no warning. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "A lot of parents will say, ‘My child never told me the issue. We were best friends. And then I got a letter saying, never contact me ever again.’" "That is a big problem. It's like people don't even know why they get cut off." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Landry noted that recognizing possible warning signs should prompt honest self-reflection, not just concern about the other person’s behavior. "If there is an imminent estrangement, dig deep," she advised. "Do you have a part? If so, is there a chance of rectifying it before it occurs?"

articles.title: Does ‘Falling Back’ an Hour Hurt Your Heart? A Doctor Shares Tips to Get Through
articles.summary: Daylight saving time ends Sunday, providing an extra hour of sleep. Doctor explains what that means for heart health and how to adjust as clocks fall back.
articles.body: Daylight saving time can be hard on the heart when people lose an hour of sleep in the spring, but there’s another period of adjustment coming this weekend. Clocks “fall back” one hour on Sunday, Nov. 1, as daylight saving time ends and standard time begins, adding an extra hour to that day. Doctors are clear about what to do with that bonus 60 minutes. Heart Health Tip of the Day: Make the Most of the Extra Hour of Sleep This is your opportunity to catch up on slumber. “Try to make use of the full extra hour, as research indicates folks only make use of about 60% of that extra time, averaging around 36 minutes of extra sleep,” Dr. Mike Varshavski, a family medicine physician, tells TODAY.com. Most people don’t take advantage of the extra hour of sleep, the Harvard Health Letter confirms, noting “’fall back’ doesn’t equal sleep gain.” Gaining an hour of sleep, especially in a sleep-deprived society, is not problematic for the heart, he adds, noting that some evidence suggests it may even be cardioprotective by lowering fight-or-flight activation, blood pressure and overall physiologic stress. Why It Matters Every clock adjustment is a jolt for the body’s circadian rhythm, or internal clock, which can disrupt sleep routines. The March transition, when clocks “spring forward” and people lose an hour of sleep, is particularly rough with an increase in heart attacks and strokes in the days following the time change, the American Heart Association noted. Fewer adverse effects come with the fall transition back to standard time, which is “more aligned with our circadian rhythm,” experts say. But it still throws off the daily routine for a few days. It’s worth giving your body a little extra TLC during this time and be cognizant things may feel a little different. How to Get Started Plan ahead and start adjusting your nighttime routine by 10 to 20 minutes a few days before the transition to standard time, Varshavski advises. When it comes to setting a consistent bedtime, it’s usually better to focus on the wake-up time, he adds. As always, eat healthy food, exercise and get some sunlight in the morning, which helps regulate the body’s circadian rhythm. “Think about health holistically. There are other healthy habits to conquer during this time,” Varshavski says. TODAY’s Expert Tip of the Day series is all about simple strategies to make life a little easier. Every Monday through Friday, different qualified experts share their best advice on diet, fitness, heart health, mental wellness and more.
